items.title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.original_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_description: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer Claims ITL Editorial Team Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:19 Chief claims officers must transform their departments into AI-native ground-truth engines or risk becoming the bottleneck in enterprise transformation. October 7, 2026 Image For decades, the mandate of the chief claims cfficer was relatively clear: build a strong organization to investigate claims, control costs, manage litigation, negotiate settlements, and deliver fair outcomes. That mandate is no longer sufficient. The 2027 chief claims officer has a much bigger job: build the insurer's ground-truth engine—an AI-native operation that produces superior outcomes, industrializes negotiation excellence, and converts what claims learns into intelligence for the entire enterprise. This is not simply about using AI to make legacy claims processes more efficient. AI is turning insurance into an information business—and the most important ground truth in that business is generated in claims. Claims reveal what actually happened to the risks the insurer underwrote, what drove the loss, and what ultimately determined its economic outcome. To compete in an AI world, insurers will need to capture that ground truth, make it machine-readable, and use it to improve underwriting, pricing, reserving, and portfolio management. That puts claims—and the chief claims officer—on the front line of this unprecedented transformation. A new competitive environment Claims officers in traditional claims organizations face urgent and pressing competition from two sources at once. On one side is an increasingly industrialized plaintiff bar. On the other side is a new generation of AI-native insurers, poised to move forward. On the first side, consider Morgan & Morgan. The personal-injury giant says it has invested roughly $300 million in technology and AI and plans at least $1 billion more over the next decade. Its proprietary MX2 platform supports medical-record extraction, case research, document generation, demand letters, and trial preparation, while Injury.com digitally acquires and qualifies potential claims. Private equity is adding fuel, investing in personal-injury platforms to scale technology, analytics, marketing and standardized operations. The plaintiff bar is turning claim development and negotiation from individual craftsmanship into an industrial system. On the second side, a new generation of AI-native insurers is being built without decades of legacy technology, workflows and organizational baggage. Companies such as Corgi are attempting to build insurance businesses from inception around modern data architectures, AI agents and technology-speed iteration. McKinsey has warned that AI-native insurance businesses can increasingly build and refine products in weeks while incumbents remain calibrated to annual planning cycles and multi-year transformations. Legacy insurers are being squeezed from both directions: out-innovated by the plaintiff bar in the contest over outcomes and potentially out-architected by AI-native insurers in the contest over how insurance itself operates. Claims sits directly in the middle. That changes the requirements of its leader. 1. Level the playing field with the plaintiff bar The plaintiff bar has largely approached AI as a weapon for improving economic outcomes. Carriers have largely approached it as a tool for workflow efficiency. AI-powered demand packages are working. Carriers are only beginning to experiment seriously with the corresponding AI-powered offer package. Meanwhile, sophisticated plaintiff organizations are accumulating data, developing proprietary AI and attracting enormous capital. The plaintiff bar is both the threat and the proof point. They are investing their own money—and increasing institutional capital—because better case development, persuasion, and negotiation improve their economics. The CCO must build institutional capabilities that can match increasingly industrialized counterparties. 2. Institutionalize negotiation excellence Most carriers have some excellent negotiators. That is no longer enough. If negotiation materially affects indemnity outcomes, it cannot remain an individual skill distributed unevenly across thousands of claims professionals. The organization should know who its elite negotiators are, why they outperform and how those behaviors can be replicated. Carriers that cannot identify, measure and reproduce negotiation excellence do not really possess a negotiation capability. They possess individual negotiators. The CCO must turn individual excellence into measurable institutional capability. 3. Stop putting AI band-aids on pre-AI claims operations Many carriers can produce an impressive list of AI-centric projects: summarize a file, extract information, draft correspondence, analyze a demand, route work, search notes, or give adjusters Copilot. Those applications can create real value. But old process plus an AI tool means slightly better old process. McKinsey has warned about layering new technology onto legacy insurance operating models. BCG similarly distinguishes between deploying AI into existing processes and reshaping workflows around AI. The CCO must redesign the operating model, not merely automate the existing one. 4. Build machine-first claims The traditional claim file was built primarily for humans. Documents, notes, emails, medical records, and litigation materials accumulate while experienced professionals gradually construct an understanding of what happened. In an AI-native operation, every claim should progressively become a machine-readable representation of the claim—the people, events, evidence, injuries, allegations, relationships, negotiations and outcomes. That structured claim becomes the substrate on which specialized AI agents can continuously reason. Instead of occasionally asking AI to summarize a file, machines continuously read, structure, monitor, compare, detect, and prepare. The CCO must make claims machine-readable while elevating, not diminishing, human judgment and action. 5. Build and lead a hybrid workforce The future claim officer will have two kinds of capacity at their disposal: human expertise and machine intelligence. AI agents will increasingly read, structure, monitor, research, compare, detect, analyze and prepare. Humans will increasingly concentrate on judgment, investigation, strategy, creativity, empathy, supervision, accountability and negotiation. That will make exceptional claims professionals more important, not less. Imagine an elite negotiator supported by agents that continuously understand the evidence, medical history, venue, plaintiff counsel, negotiation history, and comparable outcomes. The machine handles much of the cognitive preparation. The human concentrates on what exceptional humans do best: think, strategize, persuade, read the counterparty, exercise judgment, and negotiate. The CCO must become the architect of human and machine capacity—designing how each works together to produce better outcomes. 6. Make every negotiation a learning event A sophisticated plaintiff demand should eventually meet an equally sophisticated carrier response. But the bigger opportunity comes afterward. Every demand, analysis, strategy, offer, response, counteroffer, and outcome must become institutional knowledge in the same way that the plaintiff bar is institutionalizing these events. Which plaintiff firms consistently outperform? Which strategies work against them? Which facts change settlement value? Which negotiators outperform expectations? Where does the organization systematically overpay? Every negotiation should make the next negotiation smarter. The CCO must ensure every claim and negotiation makes the organization smarter. 7. Elevate claims into the insurer's ground-truth engine This is where the transformation extends beyond claims. Underwriting begins with hypotheses about risk. Pricing quantifies them. Reserving updates them. Claims discovers what was actually true. Claims learns what caused the loss, how injuries developed, what evidence mattered, how attorneys behaved, which defenses and negotiation strategies worked, and what the risk ultimately cost. Yet much of that knowledge remains trapped in PDFs, notes, litigation files and the heads of experienced claims professionals. Claims should continuously produce structured intelligence that flows into underwriting, pricing, reserving, risk, reinsurance and portfolio management. The claim is no longer simply something to resolve and close. It is one of the insurer's richest proprietary information assets. The CCO must turn claims knowledge into enterprise intelligence—making the claims organization the feedback loop that allows the entire enterprise to learn. 8. Don't let claims become the transformation bottleneck This may be the requirement that matters most to the rest of the C-suite. A legacy insurer can modernize distribution, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. But if its richest source of ground truth remains trapped inside a document-centric, human-first claims operation moving through multi-year transformation cycles, the rest of the enterprise eventually hits a wall. AI-native competitors do not have to unwind decades of organizational architecture before redesigning how humans, machines and data work together. Incumbents do. That makes speed itself a competitive capability. The modern CCO must protect the integrity of a massive, consequential operation while simultaneously making it capable of continuous change. The plaintiff bar is moving at technology speed. AI-native competitors are being built for technology speed. Claims cannot continue moving at insurance speed. The CCO must ensure claims leads rather than constrains the insurer's AI transformation. The mandate has changed None of these requirements eliminates the traditional responsibilities of the CCO. Claims still must be handled fairly; customers, regulatory obligations, litigation, reserves and operational discipline still matter. But those responsibilities are increasingly table stakes. Sophisticated plaintiff organizations are industrializing the pursuit of settlement dollars while AI-native insurers are being architected as technology-speed information businesses. Between them sits a claims organization that, at many incumbents, was designed for another era. That creates both a threat and an extraordinary opportunity. Carriers that generate that ground truth better, negotiate from it more effectively, make it machine-readable and distribute it throughout the enterprise will possess something more valuable than a more efficient claims department. They will possess a continuously learning insurance enterprise. As chief claims officers enter 2027, the question is no longer whether their departments will use more AI. It is whether they can transform their departments into a competitive advantage rather than the bottleneck preventing the enterprise from changing with it. Taylor Smith John Burge

items.rss_description: A Novel Approach to Preventing Water Damage IOT RyanMeyer Mon, 09/28/2026 - 16:00 LeakBot provides a sensor that detects tiny, even hidden leaks so they can be repaired months before they would cause significant damage. September 28, 2026 Image Paul Carroll As part of our push for insurers to increasingly adopt a Predict & Prevent model, I’ve been tracking water sensors for a long time. Leaks cause so much damage to homes. The sensors I’ve tracked have improved a lot, getting ever closer to the point where they make clear economic sense—where the savings from prevention exceed the cost of deployment. You have a different approach that has convinced a lot of insurers that you’ve passed that tipping point. To start us off, would you tell us what your approach looks like? That unit can detect a leak anywhere on the main water system, and it's sensitive down to about a teaspoon of water per minute—we say five milliliters per minute in the U.K. It's about 100 times more sensitive than an ultrasonic sensor, which is the next best approach without physically cutting the pipe. If we detect a leak, we'll tell you what to do through the app. If it looks like you've got a hidden problem, we'll send a LeakBot plumber to the house. And there's absolutely no charge for that—it's all paid for by the insurance company. Paul Carroll A lot of leak sensors shut off the water automatically when they detect a problem. Why do you take a different approach? Craig Foster This is a key point. We're detecting really small leaks before they've had a chance to build up and cause a big problem. The first response is often what you've said, Paul: "Wait a minute. Don't you need a shutoff valve to stop the damage?" But the important insight is that plumbing rarely goes from being fine to a sudden high release of water without any problem in between—unless there's some kind of DIY mistake or a pipe freezes and thaws, and there’s a break. In those instances, we'll alert the customer and say, "Hey, water's running. Do you know what it is?" But we deliver the ROI for partners by catching leaks much, much earlier—months earlier. Leaks start very small, with drips, then get exponentially worse over time, but you don't know about it as the homeowner because the leaks are hidden. They're in cavity walls. They're in ceilings. They're down the back of cupboards. They're in places where you just don't see them. Carriers will tell us, "We get a lot of claims on water heaters. They’ll fail and suddenly leak gallons and gallons of water in a basement, and it's a $40,000 claim. You wouldn't be able to shut the water off in time." But we’ll show them that that sort of problem is a really high percentage of what our plumbers fix every day. We'll get alerted to a leak, go to the home, and find a pinhole leak on the pipe into the water heater—sometimes with just a bit of green calcification and a tiny drip. It could keep getting exponentially worse until there is a faster flow, and then the pipe pops. That would normally be the first time the homeowner knows there’s a problem—but we’ve fixed it. In the U.S., it's almost like carriers have been trained that a shutoff valve is the gold standard. They’re expensive, so carriers will sometimes talk to us as they look for a cheaper alternative. But we convince them that we’re not just more cost-effective, we’re a better solution. Paul Carroll Once you know a home is leaking a teaspoon of water a minute, how do you find the problem? Homes are big places. Craig Foster If we're detecting a small leak, we'll alert the customer and guide them through steps to check common causes. Maybe they’ve been in the garden and haven’t completely turned the hose off. Or they’ve had guests, who’ve used a bathroom they don’t use all the time, and the tap is dripping. 60% of the time, customers solve the problem themselves. If the customer says, "I can't see what it is. Can you help me?" then we suggest booking one of our plumbers. The genesis for the company was actually as part of a home services group in the U.K. that also has a big business in the U.S. called HomeServe. So we have a heritage in plumbing and brought a lot of expertise with us when we spun out. Our plumbers use thermal imaging cameras, and we have patented technology that pressure tests the property. The plumbers will find and fix a problem, then run the test again. Sometimes they fix one thing, sometimes two—I think the record is 11 things, in a big house in Virginia. They'll keep going until the property is leak-free. We train our plumbers to think like adjusters. They take pictures of what they fixed, before and after. And let’s say they fix a hidden feed into a tap or a toilet in an upstairs bathroom—they go to the room below and take a wide photograph of that space. All that information goes into partner portals so our insurance partners can review the evidence of the risks we're removing from properties. If you show these reports to anyone in the claims team, they recognize them instantly. The other day, someone at a carrier partner who used to work in claims looked at a photo of a basement where we fixed a leak and said, "Oh, man, that would have been a $30,000 claim." Why so expensive? He said, "Look at the floor—it's continuous all the way through that finished basement. If that gets damaged, even a small section, we have to replace the whole floor." Even before we get to the statistical evidence about the ROI we provide, this all feels right to the claims guys. We’re fixing the things that definitely do cause them claims. Paul Carroll The economic argument for prevention is always complex. Homeowners save on the deductible and avoid enormous hassle, while the carrier saves money by preventing losses and presumably improves retention by increasing customer satisfaction. But how do you assemble those four, sometimes amorphous benefits into a case that convinces a carrier to distribute leak detection devices for free? Craig Foster We have a very simple proposition. Our solution delivers a straight return on investment on the claims saved versus the cost of deployment. And we make that return easy to measure. We charge a single fee for an active device in an insured home: $60 a year. That fee includes everything. There's no extra hardware fee. There's no shipment fee. There’s no fee for customer support, including us sending a plumber into the home as many times as we need to get that property leak-free. The carrier only pays for the devices that are installed. If you ship 100 to your customers, and 70 get installed, we take the hit on the other 30. So all you need to know is if you're going to save more than $60 in underwriting costs a year per home. This is really the nub of our recent white paper . We've proved, time and time again, based on a highly statistically relevant sample, that we can reduce the frequency of leak claims by 60%. In the U.S., on average, that delivers a 40% return on investment, and that’s just based on frequency. There is a severity benefit, too, because we tend to take out the bigger claims. Customer satisfaction is also fantastic. Nevertheless, we put all that to the side because the ROI case is clear and easy to measure. Paul Carroll I found the analysis in the white paper to be quite sophisticated. For instance, it takes into account the bias that can occur during pilot programs due to self-selection—something many companies conveniently ignore. It also acknowledges that claims actually increase early on as previously unknown problems are discovered and solved, before declining over time. But you’ll keep learning as you continue to scale, so I wonder both where you are now and where you expect to be in the next two or three years. Craig Foster We're now up to 360,000 exposure years of data—devices active in homes where we've been consistently sending plumbers and generating thousands and thousands of claims mitigation reports. We ask partners for as much information as they can provide about claims still being experienced by the cohort with LeakBot sensors, and we’re iterating to make the system better. The biggest issue, by the way, is with customers who got an alert but didn’t think there was a problem and didn’t call out our plumbing service Paul Carroll I imagine you see some interesting patterns. Craig Foster We've learned a lot about different cohorts and different countries. For example, pipes in 1970s Denmark are particularly high-risk because of the type of plastic used. Victorian properties in the U.K. are very risky because they've got old copper plumbing and lots of bathrooms. We work with NFU, the National Farmers Union, and we're fixing leaks in these huge farmhouses in the middle of the countryside. They've all got like six bathrooms, and the plumbing is 100 years old, so they're just full of leaks. Paul Carroll Have you explored joint marketing opportunities with other companies in adjacent spaces, beyond your existing carrier partnerships? Craig Foster Bob Marshall [CEO of Ting Labs, whose device detects electrical problems that can cause fires] and I have met many times and exchanged notes a lot. There are lots of synergies. For one, Bob’s success with Ting has changed the mindset of carriers. We're moving past, “Predict & Prevent sounds like it might be a good idea, but will it really work? Let's maybe do a small test." The mindset is now, “Predict & Prevent is the future.” It's now a question of what the real solutions are that actually deliver a return on investment. Our partners have found that if a customer has already installed a Ting, they don’t even need to ask if the customer would like a LeakBot. They just send one, and we get the same installation rate as through the opt-in process. Ting is a great solution, and their success helps us, as well. Paul Carroll Any final thoughts? Craig Foster The question from U.S. carriers was, “You're a U.K. company. Can you really get this working in the U.S.?” We're now in 26 states, and we've got the actuarial evidence in the U.S. We're not reliant on the European data, although it's, funnily enough, remarkably consistent. So we very much see that tipping point, and the U.S. is the key for us in terms of the scale of the opportunity. That's the focus for the business going forward. Paul Carroll Thanks, Craig. items.title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?

items.rss_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_description: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/05/2026 - 17:40 The employment report for September in the U.S. showed a loss of 7,000 jobs in financial services. Insurance, alone, has now lost 90,000 jobs since May 2025. What's going on? I have a theory, and it's not about artificial intelligence. If I'm right, hiring in insurance will stay in the doldrums for a while. Let's have a look. As Insurance Business reports , the industry still employs a massive 2.9 million people in the U.S., but claims jobs are down a hefty 21% over the past year, while life and health is off 4%, P&C down 1.7%, and agents and brokers down 1.1%. The losses are accelerating: The article says, " Insurers lost about 1,900 jobs a month on average in 2025 and roughly 6,900 a month so far in 2026." A thorough analysis in Barron's mostly attributes the job losses to cost-cutting under pressure. Barron's notes that the surge in rates following the COVID disruption has slowed. In addition, government subsidies for healthcare have been cut even as claims costs keep increasing. In the face of pressure on both premiums and expenses, insurers have had to become more efficient, Barron's says. It does say AI has played a role by automating tasks but doesn't treat that as a huge issue just yet (and I've been arguing for months that the fears of job losses to AI are overstated). You could also add the effects of the "silver tsunami" -- the oft-quoted projection by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2021 that 400,000 insurance professionals would retire by the end of 2026. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. items.extracted_text: Tesla Faces Probe Over Claim of Robotaxis Speeding in School Zones Article 0 Comments Tesla Inc. is facing scrutiny from U.S. auto-safety regulators over whether its driverless taxis exceed posted speed limits near schools, a new hurdle for the automaker’s slow-growing robotaxi service. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it’s evaluating the claim that Tesla Cybercab and Model Y vehicles using automated systems drive too fast in active school zones. The move stems from a recently filed petition that offers video of several incidents as supporting evidence, according to documents posted Monday to NHTSA’s website. Related: Tesla Is Browbeating The EU to OK Its Full Self-Driving Tech. The Pressure Is Working The preliminary probe covers an estimated 1,000 vehicles from the 2026 model year, NHTSA said. The agency has not yet decided whether to grant or deny the petitioner’s request for a full investigation. Tesla didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Bloomberg. The new probe threatens to further complicate Tesla’s plan to expand its robotaxi service, which launched last year but still is limited to a small number of cities and in some instances uses human safety monitors. Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk sees the business as central to his effort to reorient the car manufacturer around futuristic business lines such as autonomous driving and humanoid robots. Related: Tesla’s Supervised Self-Driving System Often Misreads Speed Limits, Belgian Safety Group Finds NHTSA has a separate investigation underway into the process and technical data Tesla relied on when the company self-certified the Cybercab, a two-seat car with no steering wheel or foot pedals. Complaints over conduct in school zones are recall issues that Waymo, the leading robotaxi operator, has had involving school buses. NHTSA opened an investigation late last year into the Alphabet Inc.-owned company, followed by a similar probe several months later from the National Transportation Safety Board, over incidents in which Waymo vehicles failed to fully slow or stop for school buses. items.rss_description: TESTING focus newsletter grant Thu, 10/01/2026 - 15:37 some summary here October 1, 2026 View this email in your browser | Forward to a colleague ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. This month, we're focusing on IT Ops: Change Management FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. continue reading > Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. When you bring in AI—we should be more nimble. read the full interview > MORE ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT Change Management Is Changing by Melissa Palmer Change management can no longer be viewed as a one-time project discipline. It must become an organizational capability. items.extracted_text: Evolving captives becoming strategic platforms for attracting third-party capital: Aon - Artemis.bm Evolving captives becoming strategic platforms for attracting third-party capital: Aon - Artemis.bm Evolving captives becoming strategic platforms for attracting third-party capital: Aon 13th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Captives are rapidly evolving from risk retention vehicles into strategic capital access platforms, which in turn is beginning to attract third-party capital, according to broker Aon, who emphasises that captive owners are increasingly partnering with external investors to unlock capacity that supports growth initiatives and long-term resilience. In a recent article, the broker underscores that captives today offer much more than an opportunity to reduce insurance costs and retain risk, noting that they are now being widely used to help businesses make strategic decisions around capital deployment and long-term resilience. Aon also added that the evolving role of captives reflects a key challenge facing business leaders. “Risks are changing faster than available insurance capacity. Losses from growing natural catastrophe, cyber and litigation exposures add pressure to balance sheets. In response, insurers are deploying capital more selectively, at times reducing line sizes and capacity. The resulting supply-demand imbalance has widened the gap between the risks organizations need to finance and the protection available through traditional markets,” the broker explained. In addition, the broker highlighted that market leaders utilise captives to bridge this gap and strengthen their broader risk financing strategies. Besides filling coverage gaps, captives also allow organisations to aggregate enterprise-wide exposures, access new sources of capital and unlock risk transfer solutions, such as insurance-linked securities (ILS). Within a volatile risk environment, the broking group observed that key market participants are increasingly gravitating toward financing structures that deliver liquidity, expedited recovery capabilities, and enhanced predictability in the aftermath of loss occurrences. In essence, captives function as a notable conduit to these mechanisms, enabling businesses to integrate parametric, reinsurance, and other alternative risk transfer methodologies into a single risk financing framework. “The growth of ILS and other structured capital solutions is creating new ways to finance risk. Captives can help organizations access these sources of capital by serving as a bridge between enterprise exposures and investors willing to assume specific risks,” Aon explained. The broker added: “Some of the most innovative captive strategies are beginning to attract third-party capital. items.original_title: South Korea, Japan Buffeted By Hacks As AI Lowers Bar For Cybercriminals
items.rss_title: South Korea, Japan Buffeted By Hacks As AI Lowers Bar For Cybercriminals
items.rss_description: South Korean and Japanese companies are racing to strengthen cyber defenses after a wave of attacks that cybersecurity experts say are highlighting how AI may be lowering the bar for criminals with limited technical skills. Nine South Korean banks and …
items.extracted_text: South Korea, Japan Buffeted By Hacks As AI Lowers Bar For Cybercriminals Article 0 Comments South Korean and Japanese companies are racing to strengthen cyber defenses after a wave of attacks that cybersecurity experts say are highlighting how AI may be lowering the bar for criminals with limited technical skills. Nine South Korean banks and two mega-churches are probing cyberattacks that may have involved AI tools, while Japanese companies including Daiwa Securities, SoftBank Corp and the Lawson convenience store chain have been hit by a recent surge in cyber incidents. Authorities are still investigating whether and how AI was used in many of the breaches. But cybersecurity specialists say the technology is helping attackers automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect. “AI doesn’t get tired… My view is that Japan is essentially being subjected to carpet bombing,” said Nobuo Miwa, president of Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm S&J Corp. Japan recorded more cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI. Incidents rose to 86 in September, up about 18% from August and 37% from July. The rise suggests attackers have crossed a threshold in “effort, motivation and technical capability,” while AI has largely erased language and other barriers that once hindered foreign hackers, Miwa said. U.S. cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said a suspected 26-year-old China-based attacker behind the South Korean bank incidents would probably not have been able to carry out the campaign without AI assistance. The individual, whom CrowdStrike assessed was pursuing financial gain, used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic’s Claude Code, according to the company. “While (the hacker’s) capabilities were not terribly sophisticated they were effective,” said Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike’s senior vice president of counter adversary operations. Hard-To-Detect Attacks AI-powered tools are also making it harder for defenders to spot suspicious behavior, said Choi Kyoungjin, director of the Center for AI, Data and Policy at Gachon University near Seoul. “With general-purpose AI models, even ordinary users with malicious intent can ask the system to look for vulnerabilities and it will do much of that work for them,” he said. South Korea reported 1,236 cyber incidents in the first half of the year, up 20% from a year earlier. While server hacking cases fell, reports of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and ransomware rose 56.7% and 76.8% respectively, according to government data. The South Korean bank incidents underscored the need for stronger security controls and more rigorous testing as AI evolves, Meyers said. “The genie is out of the bottle, so to speak.” Although the breaches have not yet resulted in material financial losses, risks could increase if stolen data is used in phishing or similar text-message “smishing” campaigns, Karen Wu, senior analyst at Fitch, wrote in a note. “We expect the incidents to result in regulatory penalties, customer compensation costs, and a sector-wide increase in cybersecurity spending,” Wu said. Defences Need Their Own Breakthrough Warnings about AI’s growing role in cybercrime are increasingly coming from the technology’s developers. Alphabet’s Google and Anthropic have both warned that AI-assisted attacks are becoming more common globally. “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited,” John Hultquist, the chief analyst at Google’s Threat Intelligence Group, said last month. Regulators in Japan and South Korea have begun responding. South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has directed financial industry associations, regulators and affected executives to complete a 12-point cybersecurity self-assessment. In Japan, digital transformation minister Toshiharu Furukawa convened a meeting of ministries and agencies on Thursday following the recent attacks. The National Cybersecurity Office plans to issue warnings to businesses. S&J’s Miwa said he expected elevated levels of cyberattacks to persist. “The attackers have experienced a breakthrough that has rendered many of the old assumptions obsolete,” he said. “Our defenses need their own breakthrough as well.” (Additional reporting by Maggie Grether and Joyce Lee in Seoul, Chang-ran Kim in Tokyo and Raphael Satter in Washington Writing by Brenda Goh Editing by Sam Nussey, Miyoung Kim and Jamie Freed) Copyright 2026 Reuters. items.original_title: Army Report Cites Systematic Failures in Helicopter And Jet Collision That Killed 67
items.rss_title: Army Report Cites Systematic Failures in Helicopter And Jet Collision That Killed 67
items.rss_description: The collision of an American Airlines regional jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport last year that killed 67 people was the result of several systemic failures, according to a U.S. Army investigative report …
items.extracted_text: Army Report Cites Systematic Failures in Helicopter And Jet Collision That Killed 67 Article 0 Comments The collision of an American Airlines regional jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport last year that killed 67 people was the result of several systemic failures, according to a U.S. Army investigative report seen by Reuters. The previously undisclosed report completed in May made a series of safety recommendations and said the key factor was two broken radio transmissions resulting in the helicopter crew not receiving critical details from air traffic control. The report also found a number of other issues including technical issues with the Black Hawk and a pattern of helicopter crews failing to fly semiannual minimum hours. It said many helicopters in the Army battalion — including the one in the January 2025 collision — did not have Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance systems. The report also said Army work with the Federal Aviation Administration on helicopter incidents in the Washington area before the collision was lacking and a working group “did not discuss airspace violations, near-miss reports, or pilot deviations.” National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy said in an October 1 letter to the Army that it had made significant progress in addressing its recommendations from the collision. It added, however, that it needed to do more work as “the Army’s aviation safety system failed to consistently detect, interpret, and act on signals of latent hazards, resulting in degraded safety assurance, organizational learning, and safety culture.” The NTSB report on the crash in January found a series of failures by the FAA were largely responsible for the deadliest US aviation disaster in more than two decades. The Army report noted that the helicopter was not providing key safety location data, known as ADS-B Out, due to improper maintenance. After the incident, the Army issued an urgent safety message to inspect all Army aircraft transponders to ensure ADS-B Out functionality, and all 3,600 Army helicopters were inspected by July 2025. The report also noted the Army had not addressed issues that led to the helicopter providing inaccurate altitude data and proposed a series of recommendations to address the issue. It also said the Army needs more advanced night vision equipment for pilots. The Army report also faulted FAA air traffic control for using “non-standard terminology for directing air traffic and providing incomplete traffic advisories.” The FAA did not immediately comment. The Army said in a statement on Thursday that it has implemented stronger training and surveillance checks and completed new helicopter safety inspections, and testing on altitude awareness. It also said it was pursuing an FAA data-sharing agreement to help identify potential midair collision risks. The report also called for improved training for military pilots around Washington and Baltimore commercial airports and for reviews of Army helicopter operations near major cities in the United States, South Korea, Japan and Germany. Congress is still debating aviation safety legislation after lawmakers passed competing versions. The family of First Officer Sam Lilley, who was killed in the collision, said the Army report shows “the system failed everyone that night. The Army’s report acknowledges failures involving known altimeter issues, near-miss reporting, training, risk mitigation and safety culture.” (Reporting by Shepardson Editing by Mark Porter and Bill Berkrot) Copyright 2026 Reuters. items.extracted_text: Swiss Re says increased reinsurance supply a positive, will align alt capital where it makes sense - Artemis.bm Swiss Re says increased reinsurance supply a positive, will align alt capital where it makes sense - Artemis.bm Swiss Re says increased reinsurance supply a positive, will align alt capital where it makes sense 13th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Speaking ahead of the 2026 Baden-Baden gathering, Leopoldo Camara, Head of P&C Reinsurance Northern, Central & Eastern Europe at Swiss Re outlined that more reinsurance capital is needed in the market to address growing, interconnected risks, while also emphasising that the reinsurer will use its deep risk expertise to align alternative capital where it makes sense. “We see more capital flowing into the markets and into the reinsurance industry, and we think that is actually good news because more capital is needed to address the growing risks that we all need to deal with,” Camara explained. Moreover, Camara underscored that different types of capital play different roles across the industry, highlighting the company’s long-standing commitment to reinsurance and its combination of capital with deep risk expertise. “Our capital, the Swiss Re capital, is committed to the industry for a very long time. It is here to do multi-line reinsurance. So, we do life and health and P&C, we do short tail and long tail,” the executive said. “The core business proposition of our capital, the core mandate is on the right side of the balance sheet. So, we’re here to play to pay claims. That’s our main promise: paying claims,” Camara continued. “And we issue this promise, bringing alongside capital, deep risk expertise that we have acquired over more than 100 years. And this deep risk expertise, in our view, is absolutely indispensable to arrange risk transfer in a sustainable way, to help mitigate the risk, to actually measure and quantify the risk, to develop new risk transfer approaches, and also to align alternative capital when this makes sense. “So, this is our kind of capital. That’s the kind of capital we’re bringing to Baden-Baden, and we actually see that our capital is in high demand.” On the demand side, Camara noted that Swiss Re was seeing increasing amounts of systemic risk, with exposures becoming more interconnected and therefore more systemic. The executive identified four key factors driving this trend: larger individual risks, intensified geographic clustering, enhanced integration of supply chain networks, and growing digital and social networks that amplify risk propagation. “Larger individual risks, the prime example that comes to mind are data centers, where we see insured value concentrations in excess of billions, sometimes even tens of billions, in very small, limited locations. So, increasing amounts of large risk concentration,” Camara added. Going back to alternative capital, Camara highlighted during the Q&A portion of the briefing, that Swiss Re has a long-standing track record in the space, through the use of its third-party capital markets focused Alternative Capital Partners (ACP) division. “Swiss Re has a long-standing track record in a unit called Alternative Capital Partners. So we’re quite used and experienced in also deploying that kind of capital or supporting that kind of capital with what we bring to the table to enable alternative capital to actually take on risk,” the executive said. items.extracted_text: ‘Unusual’ Isaias Brings Winds, Downed Trees but Fewer Claims Than Expected Article 0 Comments Lots of trees and fences were down, with some roof damage to homes, businesses and vehicles, and flooding and tornadoes in parts of western North Carolina. But overall, the insured losses from Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle Friday night, are shaping up to be less than feared—and about one-tenth as costly as 2018’s Hurricane Michael, a Category 5 storm that hit east of where Isaias came ashore. Michael cost insurers about $9 billion in Florida claims in 2018, or about $12 billion in today’s dollars. “So, about a tenth of that would make Isaias a billion-dollar storm,” said Melissa Burt DeVriese, president of Florida-domiciled Security First Insurance. She based her numbers partly on estimates from Karen Clark & Co., the hurricane modeling and analytics firm. Official claims numbers had not yet been reported Monday by the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. The office has given insurers two deadlines: Oct. 13 and Oct. 15, to report claims data using the simplified catastrophe reporting form. The Cooks’ home in Pensacola (IJ photo) Isaias was the first hurricane of the Atlantic season when it came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane near the resort city of Destin, Florida. Weather services and local officials had expected the Destin area to take the brunt of the wind and storm surge since it was in the path of the eastern eyewall, which historically has proven to be where the strongest winds and surge are found. The storm, which had spun up unexpectedly in the Gulf of Mexico early last week, brought its highest recorded winds—117 mph—to the Pensacola area, along with relatively small storm surge. News reports suggested that rare “sting jet” winds may have played a role, sending violent gusts along the western side of the eye, but from the north, helping to tamp down storm surge in the Gulf and nearby bay and sound. Downed trees knocked out power to more than 670,000 customers in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi, according to news reports. Four people died in the storm, from falling trees or unventilated generators. Damage and claims reported by insureds have been relatively modest in number and severity, insurance carrier representatives, agents and adjusters said Monday. “So much of what we have seen has been below the deductible,” said Matt Mercier, national director of community associations for CBIZ, an insurance brokerage that handles a number of condo properties near Pensacola. Insurance carrier executives and claims managers gathered at an insurance claims village in Destin Monday morning. With so few policyholders showing up, they moved on to Pensacola by early afternoon. At the Pensacola insurance hub on the campus of the University of West Florida, 14 carriers set up mobile claims-handling spots, alongside representatives from the Florida Department of Financial Services. But few clients stopped by. People’s Trust Insurance was there and saw just over 400 claims in the Panhandle region, out of about 8,000 insureds, said Carlos Martinez, director of catastrophe operations for the Florida-based insurer. Universal Property & Casualty Insurance representatives said the company had fielded about 3,000 claims on about 20,000 policies in the region. Security First reported about 300 claims by Monday afternoon, out of about 15,000 policies in force in the Panhandle area. Only about five of those were considered to have severe levels of damage. “It was a smaller hurricane. But it’s not a small thing if it’s your house that gets hit by a tree,” said DeVriese. “That’s why we’re here. We have to be here for our clients.” DeVriese and six members of the Security First team showed up Monday to look at the damage to policyholder Lisa Cook’s home on the north side of Pensacola. A tree had fallen through the roof, causing damage to the roof structure and the attic. The Cooks reported the claim promptly and said they had an adjuster, a roofing company and tarp in place within 24 hours. The Security First claims team assists a policyholder in Pensacola after the storm (IJ photo) Others in the area reported that a few insureds have said a roofing company and public adjusters—wearing the roof firm’s shirt and logo—have been knocking on doors, promising that carriers will pay full replacement costs. “I said, ‘Shoo them away. Let’s check with your insurance company first on what’s covered,'” said Kelly Siler, who co-owns the Siler Insurance Agency on U.S. Highway 29 in Pensacola. Although the Siler agency office was still without electrical service Monday, three days after the tempest passed, the owners were on site, ready to assist policyholders. And before the storm hit, the Silers had posted claims phone numbers on their front window for all the carriers the agency is appointed with. “We also have paper files on all insureds, so we can help them even with the power and the computers down—we’re old school!” Siler said. Mary Jordan, owner of Gulf Coast Insurance agency in Pensacola, said she had heard from relatively few policyholders. Her own home, on a peninsula that juts into a bay, escaped damage. But the boat house and some rental property saw considerable roof damage. “Yes, we have dwelling-fire coverage” on the rental property, Jordan said. Perhaps the areas of damage that had people around town buzzing about the most were just outside Pensacola. At Portofino Island Resort, a massive, high-rise condominium complex on Pensacola Beach, lost many of its windows during the winds of Isaias. Drone video posted on social media showed bedrooms in two towers now exposed to the elements, with plate-glass windows and doors completely vanished. One insurance broker said it was surprising that the windows had blown out, but it was unclear if the towers had been built with hurricane-resistant windows. Portofino management and the resort’s insurance agents could not be reached for comment Monday. On its website, the management company said that new guest arrivals had been suspended. Northeast of Pensacola, the city of Milton also saw significant winds during the storm, up to 110 mph. The Milton High School gymnasium had much of its roof damaged. A huge section of roof was lifted off a nearby apartment complex. The Milton Quick Stop convenience store and gas station suffered heavy damage, according to social media and local news reports. Isaias was deemed more damaging than Hurricane Sally, which hit the area in 2020, but less than Hurricane Ivan, which caused widespread destruction in 2004, Keith Siler noted. The sounds of generators and chain saws could still be heard in Pensacola late Monday evening. Top photo: A collapsed porch at a home in central Pensacola. items.title: AI’s Water Strain Includes Surging Demand From Electricity Use
items.original_title: AI’s Water Strain Includes Surging Demand From Electricity Use
items.rss_title: AI’s Water Strain Includes Surging Demand From Electricity Use
items.rss_description: Data center developers have started touting new technologies that slash the amount of water needed to cool hot-running servers in drought-stressed places like Arizona. Those efforts, though, are not addressing the vast majority of the water consumed by the AI …
items.extracted_text: AI’s Water Strain Includes Surging Demand From Electricity Use Article 0 Comments Data center developers have started touting new technologies that slash the amount of water needed to cool hot-running servers in drought-stressed places like Arizona. Those efforts, though, are not addressing the vast majority of the water consumed by the AI buildout. Miles away from multiplying data centers, power plants are now consuming enormous volumes of water to generate the electricity required to run artificial intelligence, including those more efficient cooling systems. New research indicates that such indirect water consumption is rapidly growing. In a recent paper , University of Michigan researchers estimated water used offsite would boost the total annual consumption of three large AI data centers planned for the state by 14 billion gallons. “There has been much less attention to this indirect water usage, even though that oftentimes is significantly higher than the direct water usage and has impacts on watersheds and regional water resources,” said Shaolei Ren, a professor at the University of California at Riverside who studies data center water consumption . At Meta Platforms Inc., one of the only developers to publicly divulge indirect water consumption, such use accounted for about 96% of the 21 billion gallons (80 billion liters) of water the company consumed in 2024 — nearly a 120% increase from 2021 — according to its latest sustainability report . The remaining 4% was used on site, mostly at data centers, which also account for nearly all of Meta’s electricity consumption. “Transparency is a key pillar of Meta’s water stewardship program,” a spokesperson said in an email. Computing-intensive AI data centers can consume 10 times as much electricity as conventional facilities, with most of that energy needed to power servers, according to researchers. To generate that electricity, fossil-fueled and nuclear power plants need large amounts of water to produce steam to run turbines. Across the US, a growing backlash has emphasized concerns about local environmental impacts and rising electricity bills. That opposition has prompted moratoriums and other restrictions. At least 45 projects valued at nearly $68 billion were blocked or delayed between April and June, according to research firm Data Center Watch. There’s a risk data centers’ rapid growth will intensify the impact of climate-driven droughts and heat waves, which are already stressing water supplies in many places. “Demand for data centers is just skyrocketing and the truth of the matter is that the power and water facilities won’t be able to keep up,” said Kerri Hickenbottom , an associate professor of engineering at the University of Arizona who researches data center water use. Estimates of US data centers’ annual indirect water use range from 211 billion gallons (800 billion liters) in a 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study to as much as 4 trillion gallons based on a recent analysis from environmental nonprofit Ceres. That’s enough to supply between 2 million and nearly 37 million average US households per year. Developers said one reason for the lack of disclosure is that there’s no standard protocol for calculating data centers’ indirect water use. “We need industry alignment on one if we’re going to collectively report indirect water consumption,” said Brandon Oyer, head of energy and water for Amazon Web Services. Amazon.com Inc. said water efficiency at its data centers has improved by 52% since 2021, in part from deploying cooling systems that require less of it and through technology that reduces heat inside the facilities. “That is keeping both the onsite and the offsite water use as low as possible,” said Will Hewes, Amazon Web Services’ water sustainability lead. Ben Townsend, head of infrastructure strategy and sustainability at Google, said the company currently doesn’t report indirect water use but has concentrated on powering data centers with renewable energy. “With wind, solar, storage, these projects have effectively zero water footprint,” he said. Such solutions are being put to the test in drought-stressed data center hotspots such as Arizona, where water is a flash point as the Colorado River and its reservoirs dry up. The federal government in August announced a 27% cut to Arizona’s water allocation, with far more severe cuts possible if conditions continue to deteriorate. The state’s data centers are concentrated in the Phoenix area, where cities depend on the river for 20% to 50% of their water supply . AI data center projects currently being built in Arizona could spike onsite water demand to 5 billion gallons annually in coming years, Bloomberg Intelligence predicts, or 4.5% of Phoenix’s current annual water production. But the indirect water use would be orders of magnitude more, according to researchers. Michael Gertzman, a spokesperson for the Phoenix Water Services Department, said a large data center applicant must disclose its estimated onsite water consumption. Indirect water use isn’t part of the evaluation. With the southwest US suffering a record 26-year drought, and Phoenix’s summer temperatures hitting an average daily high of 108F (42C) in recent years, data center developers are turning to technology that relies on little or no onsite water, such as air-chilled coolers. There are tradeoffs, however, as removing that heat requires electricity. A 2025 study that Hickenbottom co-authored noted that in the Phoenix area, the indirect water consumption of systems using air-cooled chillers can be more than 2.5 times that of water-cooled chillers, which use more water on site. Microsoft Corp., which operates several data centers in Arizona, didn’t provide data on its indirect water use or indicate whether it calculates that consumption. The company said it has reduced the amount of water needed onsite per kilowatt-hour used at its data centers by 90% since the early 2000s. It expects to save 33 million gallons (125 million liters) annually at each of its facilities thanks to liquid cooling designs. “Our focus is on minimizing the water we use directly in the communities where we operate while maintaining highly efficient data center designs and working with utilities to help meet our power needs responsibly,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in an email. items.extracted_text: Insurance Executive Killed His Wife, Daughter, Then Himself, NJ Township Police Say Article 0 Comments A New Jersey title insurance executive shot his wife and daughter and then shot himself, according to local police and prosecutors. Montgomery Township police discovered the double homicide and suicide when responding to a call to check on the occupants of a residence on Wild Azalea Lane. Police did not identify the caller. According to officials, the officers gained entry into the residence early in the evening on Friday, October 2. They discovered two deceased adult females located within two separate bedrooms. Both victims appeared to have suffered from gunshot wounds. They also found a deceased adult male with what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The deceased male had a firearm. All three were pronounced deceased at the scene by medical personnel. A postmortem examination identified the female victims as Lora Grodnick, age 62, and Sloane Grodnick, age 24, mother and daughter and confirmed that both deaths were homicides. The deceased male was identified as David Grodnick, age 61, husband to Lora and father to Sloane. His death was confirmed a suicide. The Montgomery police along with detectives from the Somerset County Prosecutor’s Office Major Crimes Unit, the Crime Scene Investigation Unit, and medical investigators from the New Jersey Northern Regional Medical Examiner’s Office responded to investigate. The investigation remains ongoing. According to LinkedIn, David Grodnick was a title insurance expert. In May 2025, he became senior vice president and underwriting counsel at Land Services USA, LLC, based in Philadelphia, which provides real estate title and settlement services to attorneys, investors, developers, educational institutions, healthcare entities, REITs and commercial lenders. Previously he was with American Title Insurance for 20 years. Grodnick was a member of the American Bar Association, New Jersey Bar Association, Princeton Bar Association and New Jersey Land Title Association. Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: Liberty Mutual Re makes sensor-triggered parametric earthquake payout in Mexico - Artemis.bm Liberty Mutual Re makes sensor-triggered parametric earthquake payout in Mexico - Artemis.bm Liberty Mutual Re makes sensor-triggered parametric earthquake payout in Mexico 13th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Liberty Mutual Reinsurance (LM Re), part of Liberty Mutual Insurance Group, has issued a parametric payout to the Mexican federal government for the 7.3 magnitude earthquake that struck Mexico’s southern coast in July, and activated Safehub’s Shake Network trigger. The earthquake that struck Mexico’s southern coast on July 17th, 2026, triggered coverage under the government’s nationwide parametric earthquake and volcanic risk insurance program within weeks of the policy’s inception, for which LM Re has served as lead capacity provider of since June. The federal program is overseen by Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público, Mexico’s Ministry of Finance and Public Credit, and administered by Agroasemex, S.A., the Mexican state-owned insurance institution. Moreover, the policy utilises ShakeNet Parametric, Liberty Mutual Re’s (LM Re) earthquake parametric insurance and risk management technology solution, powered by Safehub’s Shake Network and the Global Earthquake Model’s (GEM) OpenQuake engine. By deploying Safehub’s propriety sensor network, the Shake Network reduces basis risk by bridging the gap between estimated models and actual ground motion. Both companies confirmed that during the earthquake event, Safehub’s sensors recorded shaking within 80 km of the epicenter, delivering critical ground-truth to facilitate a precise and rapid trigger. According to LM Re and Safehub, the Mexico program represents the largest ShakeNet Parametric deployment to date, backed by an extensive nationwide Safehub sensor network. In addition, the parametric payment also meets Mexico’s government’s goal of ensuring fiscal resilience and continuity of public services after disasters. As per the announcement, the deal was brokered by Augment Risk and domestic broker TBS. Jean-Christophe Garaix, Head of Parametrics and Agriculture at LM Re, commented: “We are pleased to support the Mexican government in its disaster preparedness program. This claim payout reflects the effectiveness of how our solution can strengthen disaster resilience at a national scale, providing support when insureds need it most. “It also showcases the growing demand for high-resolution earthquake impact data in risk transfer applications, with additional large-scale projects currently being developed in markets around the world.” Andy Thompson, CEO of Safehub, said: “Ground-truth data is the key to aligning theoretical models with real-world impact and reducing basis risk. We are proud that Safehub’s sensor network and technology enabled a rapid, objective payout for the Government of Mexico. Earthquake resilience depends on actionable, high-resolution data and delivering that precision is at the core of our mission.” In 2025, LM Re and Safehub launched a new earthquake parametric insurance solution that the pair at the time said will help reduce basis risk for parametric re/insurance policies. items.extracted_text: Delivering clear entry-to-exit for ILS structures essential for investor confidence: Artex’s Faries - Artemis.bm Delivering clear entry-to-exit for ILS structures essential for investor confidence: Artex’s Faries - Artemis.bm Delivering clear entry-to-exit for ILS structures essential for investor confidence: Artex’s Faries 12th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard While the industry has spent considerable time implementing ways that capital enters ILS vehicles, the mechanism for how it exits has often been treated as an afterthought. Artex Capital Solutions is dedicating effort towards building vehicles that provide a clear entry and a clear exit, with CEO Kathleen Faries emphasising that delivering clarity at the point of exit is essential to providing investors with full-lifecycle confidence. Earlier this year, Artex Capital Solutions, the insurance-linked securities market service provider and insurance management specialist, partnered with legacy and run-off reinsurance specialist Enstar that introduced structured exit options embedded within Artex’s ILS vehicles. As we explained at the time, this initiative was designed to solve the trapped capital issue for ILS investors, by providing mechanisms that can deliver greater certainty on exits from ILS investments, while providing liquidity and capital return. Artemis spoke to Faries at this year’s Rendez-Vous de Septembre in Monte Carlo, who explained how this structure fundamentally changes liquidity expectations for ILS investors. The CEO also outlined whether Artex expects embedded finality to become standard across the market going forwards. “I think that’s exactly what we’re aspiring to do. We’re looking to build infrastructure and structures that provide both a clear entry and a clear exit. Historically, we’ve relied on commutation language and collateral release provisions, but over time we’ve seen that those mechanisms may not provide the level of certainty some investors are looking for. This gives investors another option and greater confidence around the exit process,” Faries told Artemis. She further explained: “We want to deliver efficient infrastructure from entry to exit, and the exit component is something Artex has been focused on building for some time. “We manage many risk transfer vehicles globally including some that we own. The primary brand is Artex Axcell, which allows participants to rent a cell within our structure and access risk transfer efficiently.” For investors, having Enstar’s exit and finality solutions embedded directly into Artex Capital Solutions managed and facilitated ILS structures is a meaningful step forwards towards making these features available and making trapped capital less of, or no longer a primary hurdle at all in future ILS investment structures they allocate capital to. Furthermore, Faries also explained how amidst an influx of record-breaking catastrophe bond issuance, including a new record for first-half issuance at nearly $18 billion in H1 2026, how Artex is helping cat bond investors balance their search for yield with strict capital management. “At Artex, we view ourselves as critical infrastructure for the market. That’s how I think about what we do as a company. Our role is to provide investors with efficient access to risk across the asset class and multiple ways to deploy capital,” the CEO said. “That includes supporting catastrophe bonds, but also providing access to private transactions across property cat, casualty, specialty risks, and parametric transactions. Artex has experience and infrastructure to support the full range of structures and lines of business in the market.” Faries concludes: “Ultimately, Artex supports the market by creating efficient pathways for our risk transfer vehicles, capital to access risk in the way that best aligns with an investor’s objectives.” Read all of our interviews with ILS market and reinsurance sector professionals here . items.extracted_text: Exxon Blocked Proposal to Settle $5 Billion Kashagan Dispute Article 0 Comments ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. blocked a proposal for partners in the Kashagan oil field in Kazakhstan to make a settlement with the government over a disputed $5 billion environmental fine, according to people familiar with the matter. The status of that penalty subsequently became a key part of ExxonMobil’s negotiations with Kazakhstan on a proposal to expand production at Kashagan. The US company has told the government that a potential $80 billion new investment in the field would be contingent on settling the dispute. Since the fine was imposed in 2022, the oil majors behind the giant Kashagan field, which also include Shell Plc, TotalEnergies SE and Eni SpA, have discussed a variety of settlements for the long-contested 2.356 trillion-tenge ($5.2 billion), which is related to sulfur storage at the field. State-run KazMunayGas National Co. JSC is also a partner in the venture. Inpex Corp. and China National Petroleum Corp. have minority stakes. ExxonMobil wasn’t in favor of the most recent proposal and subsequently persuaded TotalEnergies, which had been neutral, over to its side, the people said, asking not to be named as the discussions were not public. Opposition from the two companies was enough to block a settlement, the people said. ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, KazMunayGas, Shell and Inpex declined to comment. Eni, CNPC and the North Caspian Operating Co., the joint venture that runs the project, didn’t respond to requests for comment. After several years of legal wrangling, an Atyrau-based court upheld the environmental penalty in a ruling on June 19. Kazakhstan’s Justice Ministry said in July that it had started the process to collect the fine. KazMunayGas has decided to pay its part of the fine, people told Bloomberg at the time. The companies continue to dispute the penalty in a pair of international arbitrations. NCOC “consider the sulfur fine to be without any basis and are contesting it by all available means,” according to a statement on July 23. Alongside this long-running disagreement, ExxonMobil has been pitching a new multibillion dollar investment to tap an undeveloped part of Kashagan in a joint venture with KazMunayGas. In talks with Kazakh officials, the US oil major has linked this potential development to the resolution of disputes between the Kashagan partners and the government, including the sulfur fine. items.extracted_text: Hurricane Isaias insurance industry loss estimated in $2bn - $4bn range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Hurricane Isaias insurance industry loss estimated in $2bn - $4bn range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Hurricane Isaias insurance industry loss estimated in $2bn – $4bn range: Euler ILS Partners 13th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, has placed an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion, noting there is the potential for the storm’s losses to add to aggregate structures. Euler ILS Partners explained that there is a good deal of complexity in the loss assessment process, given much of the damage occurred from localised atmospheric turbulence. Hurricane Isaias made landfall close to Destin, Florida early on Saturday morning local time, carrying Category 2 sustained winds of 105 mph and higher gusts. As we reported at the time, market sources and reinsurance broker reports all pointed to pre-landfall estimates in the low to mid-single digit billions of dollars. In a post-landfall report on the event we’ve seen, Euler ILS Partners explained and noted some complexity with the loss estimation process early after the hurricane, “We currently estimate insured losses at USD 2–4 billion. As is typical following a major hurricane landfall, uncertainty remains elevated in the initial post-event period, and industry loss estimates may be revised significantly as additional information becomes available. “Loss assessment is particularly challenging because most damage resulted from complex, highly localised atmospheric turbulence. In addition, heavy rainfall across the Southeast before landfall contributed to large numbers of trees falling onto roofs over a wide area.” The specialist ILS investment manager also stated, “Euler is actively monitoring the event and reviewing portfolio exposures. Current analysis indicates no impact on the portfolio. However, the insured losses may add to aggregate structures.” Euler ILS Partners also explained that its analysis of the hurricane has been supported by the use of its recently launched Global Alert System, a tool developed in-house and in operation since June to provide “hurricane and typhoon forecasts up to 16 days ahead, earthquake and hurricane footprints at street-level resolution, and real-time alerts for earthquakes, tsunamis, wildfires, floods, volcanic eruptions and ash clouds.” Other early loss estimates are now coming in for hurricane Isaias as well. Accuweather said the expect the hurricane will result in an, “estimated $16-20 billion in total damage and economic loss across the Gulf and the eastern United States.” Meanwhile, Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), has estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range, with the majority of losses expected to be located in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama.
